Q: How to update the value of a key in a dictionary, but only if the key already exists, without hashing the key twice? A:

Since .NET 6 there is no need to use wrappers - use GetValueRefOrNullRef from the CollectionsMarshal instead:

Gets either a reference to a TValue in the Dictionary<TKey, TValue> or a reference null if it does not exist in the dictionary.

var x = new Dictionary<string, string>{{"test", "1"}};
ref var valueRefOrNullRef = ref CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrNullRef(x, "test");
if (!Unsafe.IsNullRef(ref valueRefOrNullRef))
{
    valueRefOrNullRef = "2";
}

Console.WriteLine(x["test"]); // prints 2

UPD

Full implementation:

public static bool TryUpdate<TKey, TValue>(
    this Dictionary<TKey, TValue> source,
    TKey key,
    TValue value)
    where TKey : notnull
{
    ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull(source);
    ref var valueRefOrNullRef = ref CollectionsMarshal.GetValueRefOrNullRef(source, key);
    if (Unsafe.IsNullRef(ref valueRefOrNullRef))
    {
        return false;
    }

    valueRefOrNullRef = value;
    return true;
}

var x = new Dictionary<string, decimal> { { "test", 1 } };
Console.WriteLine(x.TryUpdate("test", 2)); // True
Console.WriteLine(x.TryUpdate("test1", 2)); // False
Console.WriteLine(x["test"]); // 2
Console.WriteLine(x.ContainsKey("test2")); // False

Note that this approach has next limitation (compared to the wrapper one):

Items should not be added or removed from the Dictionary<TKey, TValue> while the ref TValue is in use.

UPD2

Just for the funsies created a small benchmark (not ideal of course, it heavily misses at least on the string and dictionary size variance) but it seems that even for small dictionaries and small/medium string lengths approach with single access by key is faster:

Method Mean Error StdDev
BothUsingCollectionsMarshal 204.92 ns 2.008 ns 1.677 ns
BothUsingDoubleAccess 355.74 ns 5.947 ns 6.107 ns
OnlyPresentUsingCollectionsMarshal 116.19 ns 2.225 ns 2.081 ns
OnlyPresentUsingDoubleAccess 271.66 ns 5.423 ns 5.326 ns
OnlyMissingUsingCollectionsMarshal 91.20 ns 1.851 ns 1.818 ns
OnlyMissingUsingDoubleAccess 94.78 ns 1.891 ns 2.524 ns

Q: Making an Automatically Updating Table With Daily Updated Data From the Web (Excel Power Query) A:

If I'm understanding your question, you want to keep historic forecasts. You can solve for this via Self Referencing (see https://exceleratorbi.com.au/self-referencing-tables-power-query/ for more details).

In essence, load your table to Excel as it is. Then select the table and select Data > From Table/Range. This will create a new PQ of the loaded table in the workbook.

Let's call your first query (the CSV one) as "Latest", and the new one (from Excel), "Historic". In Historic, filter it to be upto Today. Then in Latest, filter it to after today. Then append Historic query into Latest query. Lastly, set it up so that Historic is a Connection only query (ie it doesn't load into the workbook).

The above assumes Observations in the past do not change over time, if they do then you'll need to do a little more tweaking like doing a Merge etc...

Tip: You can get yesterday and tomorrow's dates in PQ like so:

let
    yesterday =  Date.ToText( DateTime.Date(Date.AddDays(DateTime.LocalNow(), -1)), "yyyy-MM-dd"),
    tomorrow  =  Date.ToText( DateTime.Date(Date.AddDays(DateTime.LocalNow(),  1)), "yyyy-MM-dd"),
    Source = Csv.Document(Web.Contents("https://fems.fs2c.usda.gov/api/ext-climatology/download-nfdr-daily-summary/?dataset=all&startDate="&yesterday&"&endDate="&tomorrow&"&dataFormat=csv&stationIds=400101,159901&fuelModels=Y"),[Delimiter=",", Columns=25, Encoding=1252, QuoteStyle=QuoteStyle.None]),

Q: Need Help Making A Password Checker in C? A:

The main purpose of salt is making the use of so called "rainbow tables" impractical. The best method is to generate some random bytes whenever a new password is set, store them along the password hash in the user database and use that as salt. If for some reason the user database can't hold a proper salt, you could embed it in the username or derive it from the username. A username derived salt doesn't offer the same amount of security as a purely random salt, of course. However, ideally you're not using usernames directly (especially if they're derived from legal names, because legal names can change (marriage, etc.)), but have uniquely generated, high entropy user IDs (could be UUIDs, for example, which is what Windows has been doing since the earliest days of Windows-NT – a very good design decision IMHO), which are associated with screen handles by indirection. In that case you can use the high entropy user ID directly as salt.

Q: How to use the input's values in "always" definition? A:

INPUT[temp*8 : temp*8+8] does not work because the : range syntax requires both sides to be a constant.
What you want is to use the +: array slicing: INPUT[temp*8 +: 8] The left hand side of +: allows variables and represents the starting index. The right hand side is the width and must be a constant. For more on +: see Indexing vectors and arrays with +:

Other issues:

  1. Remove temp from the sensitivity list.
  2. temp needs to be assigned to something
  3. OUT should be assigned with non-blocking (<=) not blocking (=) since it is sequential logic.

always @(posedge ICLK) // no temp in sensitivity list
begin
  if (IENBL)
  begin
    OUT <= INPUT[temp*8 +: 8]; // non-blocking and +:
  end
end
